edges.justification: Book‑to‑market ratio is measured at the start of the year and directly influences expected 12‑month stock returns.
Earnings surprise occurs during the year and directly affects the firm’s total return over that period.
The month the fiscal year ends determines the timing of earnings announcements and valuations that drive the following year’s return.
Firm performance over the year influences institutional investors’ decisions to buy or sell shares in the following twelve months.
Leverage measured at the start of the year constrains future return potential over the next twelve months.
The overall market return during the period directly affects the individual stock’s return.
Historical performance over the five years before the start of the year provides context for future returns.
The firm’s annual return contributes to the profitability component of the quality score measured at year‑end.
Value index membership is assigned at the start of the year based on book‑to‑market and influences expected returns.
The timing of fiscal year end affects the valuation window used to calculate book‑to‑market at year‑start.
Value‑oriented firms (low book‑to‑market) attract institutional investors, leading to ownership changes after the year.
Historical returns shape market perception and valuation, thereby influencing the book‑to‑market ratio at year‑start.
Low book‑to‑market is a key component of the quality score’s value dimension.
Value index membership is assigned directly based on the book‑to‑market ratio.
The fiscal year end month determines when earnings are reported, which in turn defines the earnings surprise.
Earnings surprise alters investor sentiment, influencing institutional ownership decisions in the following year.
Forecasts incorporate past performance; past returns help determine the magnitude of earnings surprise.
Earnings surprise feeds into profitability and growth components of the year‑end quality score.
The timing of the fiscal year end can influence post‑reporting institutional investor actions.
The month of fiscal year end affects the timing of leverage reporting.
Fiscal year end month determines the period used to calculate the past‑five‑year return.
The timing of reporting influences the components of the year‑end quality score.
Fiscal year end timing can affect the valuation basis used for assigning value index membership.
Higher leverage signals higher risk, prompting institutional investors to adjust holdings.
Market return trends guide institutional portfolio adjustments after the year.
Historical performance informs institutional investment decisions in the following year.
A higher quality score attracts institutional investors, leading to ownership changes.
Value index membership influences institutional portfolio construction after the year.
Lower leverage is a safety component of the quality score.
Past performance informs the growth component of the year‑end quality score.
Historical returns may influence classification into a value index via their impact on book‑to‑market.
